title: People and introductions
objective: Introduce a person and understand basic personal information.
teaching: Use I am, you are, and he or she is. My, your and her show who something belongs to. Ask What is your name? and Where are you from? A country is not a nationality: Mexico is a country; Mexican describes a person from Mexico.
reading: Hello! My name is Eva. I am nineteen. I am from Mexico, but my friend Leo is from Chile. We are students. Our English teacher is Anna. Her classroom is small. We study on Monday and Wednesday. Leo and I are in the same class, but we are not from the same country.
comprehension: Eva says she is from Mexico; Leo is from Chile.
What do Eva and Leo share?
They are in the same class; Leo's age is not stated.
grammar: Complete with am, is or are: My name ___ Eva.
is
Name is singular, so use is.
Rewrite with she: I am a student.
She is a student.
Change I to she and am to is.
dialogue: A new student joins your class. Student: Hello, I am Ben. What is your name? You want to introduce yourself politely.
interaction: Which response introduces you?
Nice to meet you. I am Rosa.
You are from Monday.
No, the room is small.
Give your name and acknowledge the introduction.
listening: Hi, I am Sam. I am twenty. I am from Canada. My English class is on Tuesday, not Thursday. My teacher is Maria.
listening_questions: He says Tuesday and explicitly rules out Thursday.

title: Days and daily routines
objective: Understand simple routines, clock times and present-simple forms.
teaching: Use the present simple for routines. With I, say I work; with she, say she works. Use at with clock times and on with days. Do not confuse a routine with an action happening now. Before means earlier; after means later.
reading: Nora works in a cafe. She starts at eight in the morning. She has lunch at one and finishes at four. On Saturday, she does not work. She visits her brother after breakfast. They walk to the park. On Sunday, Nora stays at home and reads a book.
comprehension: She finishes at four; eight is her start time.
What does she do on Saturday?
She reads at home all day.
The Saturday routine includes visiting her brother after breakfast.
grammar: Complete: She ___ (work) in a cafe.
works
Add -s with she in an affirmative present-simple sentence.
Complete with at or on: The class starts ___ nine.
at
Use at with a clock time.
dialogue: You arrange a weekly study session. Friend: Are you free on Friday? You work on Friday, but you are free on Saturday.
interaction: Choose the useful reply.
Yes, I work every Friday.
I cannot on Friday. Is Saturday OK?
Friday is a number.
Decline the unavailable day and offer a specific alternative.
listening: I get up at seven. I usually have breakfast at home, but on Friday I eat at the station. My train leaves at eight thirty.
listening_questions: Where does the speaker eat on Friday?
Friday is an exception to the usual breakfast at home.
The train leaves at eight thirty.

title: Homes and neighbourhoods
objective: Locate everyday places and understand there is and there are.
teaching: Use there is for one thing and there are for more than one. Next to means beside. Opposite means across from. Between needs two reference points. A location tells us where something is; a direction tells us how to get there.
reading: Our street has a library, a small shop and a park. The library is opposite the shop. The park is behind the library. There are two benches in the park, but there is no cafe. My flat is next to the shop. I walk to the library because it is near my home.
comprehension: The library is opposite the shop.
What is not in the park?
The text explicitly says there is no cafe.
grammar: Complete with is or are: There ___ two benches.
are
Two benches is plural.
Complete with is or are: There ___ a shop near my home.
is
A shop is singular.
dialogue: Visitor: Excuse me, where is the library? You know it is across the street from the shop.
interaction: Choose a helpful direction.
It opens on Tuesday.
It is opposite the shop.
I like reading books.
Opposite the shop gives the requested location.
listening: The pharmacy is next to the bank. The supermarket is opposite the bank. Please meet me at the pharmacy, not at the supermarket.
listening_questions: The pharmacy is next to the bank.
Where should the listener meet the speaker?
The speaker asks to meet at the pharmacy.

title: Food and simple requests
objective: Order food politely and distinguish countable and uncountable nouns.
teaching: Use a or an with one countable item: a sandwich, an apple. Water and rice are usually uncountable; say some water or a glass of water. I would like is a polite way to request something. A price per item is not the total price.
reading: At the market, Tom buys two apples and a loaf of bread. Each apple costs one pound. The bread costs two pounds. Tom has five pounds, so he has one pound left. He wants some water, but the water stall is closed. He drinks water when he gets home.
comprehension: Two apples cost two pounds and the bread costs two more.
Why does he not buy water?
He still has one pound, but the water stall is closed.
grammar: Complete with a or an: I would like ___ apple.
an
Apple begins with a vowel sound.
Complete with some or a: Can I have ___ water?
some
Water is uncountable in this request.
dialogue: Server: What would you like? You want one sandwich and a glass of water, politely.
interaction: Choose the polite, clear order.
A sandwich and a glass of water, please.
You eat my water.
Sandwiches are next to the bank.
The request names both items and includes please.
listening: Can I have a cheese sandwich and a cup of tea, please? No sugar in the tea. I will take the sandwich away, but drink the tea here.
listening_questions: The customer orders a cup of tea.
Where will the customer eat the sandwich?
Take away means the sandwich will not be eaten in the cafe.

title: Interests and abilities
objective: Describe preferences and abilities using like and can.
teaching: Can describes ability: I can swim. The next verb stays in its base form: she can swim, not she can swims. Like describes enjoyment, not ability. I like playing tennis does not necessarily mean I play well. Use but to contrast two facts.
reading: Amir likes music. He can play the guitar, but he cannot play the piano. His sister can play the piano. On Fridays, they play music together at home. Amir also likes swimming, but he does not swim in winter. His sister does not like swimming. She likes drawing pictures.
comprehension: Amir can play the guitar but cannot play the piano.
The sister likes drawing and does not like swimming.
grammar: Correct the verb after can: She can plays the piano.
She can play the piano.
Can is followed by the base form play.
Complete with can or cannot: I do not know how to swim. I ___ swim.
cannot
Cannot expresses a lack of ability.
dialogue: A club organiser asks: Can you play the guitar for our group? You can play, but you are only free on Friday.
interaction: Choose the accurate reply.
I cannot like Friday.
Yes, but only on Friday.
No, I can play very well.
The reply confirms ability while stating availability.
listening: I enjoy cycling, but I cannot ride very far. My friend Jo can cycle fifty kilometres. We both like walking, so we walk together on Sundays.
listening_questions: The speaker assigns that ability to Jo.
What do they do together on Sundays?
They walk together because both enjoy walking.

title: Shopping and near-future plans
objective: Understand prices, demonstratives and simple plans with going to.
teaching: This and that refer to one item; these and those refer to several. This is near the speaker; that is farther away. Use am, is or are plus going to and a base verb for a plan: we are going to visit. A plan is an intention, not proof it has already happened.
reading: Lily is going to visit her aunt tomorrow. Today, she is buying a present. She sees a blue scarf for ten pounds and a green scarf for eight pounds. Her aunt likes green, so Lily buys the green scarf. She is going to travel by bus. The bus stop is near her house.
comprehension: Why does Lily choose the green scarf?
Her aunt's colour preference is the stated reason.
How is Lily planning to travel?
She is going to travel by bus; the trip is tomorrow.
grammar: Complete with this or these: ___ shoes are blue.
These
Shoes is plural, so use these.
Complete: We ___ going to visit our aunt.
are
We takes are before going to.
dialogue: Shop assistant: Would you like the blue scarf or the green one? You have decided on the green scarf.
interaction: Choose your reply.
The green one, please.
I am blue tomorrow.
They travel at eight.
The green one clearly refers back to the green scarf.
listening: Tomorrow we are going to the museum. Tickets are six pounds for adults and three pounds for students. Bring your student card. We are meeting at ten outside the entrance.
listening_questions: A student card is requested for the student ticket.
The group meets at ten outside the entrance.

title: Past events and short narratives
objective: Sequence finished events using past-simple verbs and time markers.
teaching: Use the past simple for finished events: visited, went, bought. After did or did not, use the base verb. First, then and finally organise events. Yesterday and last weekend refer to finished time. Distinguish an event from the reason for it.
reading: Last Sunday, Ella planned to visit a museum. First, she checked the opening times online. Then she caught a bus, but she left her wallet at home. She got off at the next stop and walked back. Finally, she visited the museum in the afternoon. She missed the morning tour, but she enjoyed the exhibition.
comprehension: She returned because she had left her wallet at home.
She eventually visited, but missed the morning tour.
grammar: Correct: She did not visited the museum in the morning.
She did not visit the museum in the morning.
Did not requires the base form visit.
Complete with the past of buy: I ___ a ticket yesterday.
bought
Bought is the irregular past of buy.
dialogue: Friend: Did you enjoy the museum yesterday? You enjoyed it, although you missed the tour.
interaction: Choose the relevant response.
Yes, but I missed the tour.
Yes, I go tomorrow.
No, the wallet is blue.
The reply answers the past-tense question and adds the relevant contrast.
listening: We went to the coast on Saturday. The train was cancelled, so we took a bus. We arrived at noon and ate lunch before going to the beach.
listening_questions: Why did they take a bus?
The cancellation caused the change of transport.
What did they do before the beach?
Lunch came before going to the beach.

title: Travel and arrangements
objective: Handle straightforward travel problems and understand arrangements.
teaching: Use the present continuous for a personal arrangement: I am meeting Ana tomorrow. A timetable may use the present simple: the train leaves at six. Could you...? makes a polite request. Single means one way; return includes travel back.
reading: Kai is visiting Bristol next week. He is staying with his cousin, so he does not need a hotel. His train leaves at nine, but he plans to reach the station at eight thirty. He bought a return ticket because he is coming home on Sunday. His cousin is meeting him at the station, not at the house.
comprehension: Why does Kai not book a hotel?
He is staying with his cousin.
He is sleeping on the train.
His cousin is meeting him at the station.
grammar: Complete: I ___ meeting my cousin tomorrow.
am
I takes am in the present continuous.
Complete with single or return: I need to travel there and back. I need a ___ ticket.
return
A return ticket covers both directions.
dialogue: At a station, your train has disappeared from the departure board. You want to ask an employee for help politely.
interaction: Which request fits?
You never run any trains.
Could you tell me which platform my train leaves from?
I already know the platform.
The request is polite and specifies the information needed.
listening: The six fifteen service to York will leave from platform four, not platform two. Passengers for Leeds should remain on platform two for the six thirty service.
listening_questions: The announcement changes the York platform to four.
When does the Leeds service leave?
The Leeds service is at six thirty.

title: Choices and comparisons
objective: Compare alternatives using comparatives, superlatives and enough.
teaching: Short adjectives often take -er: cheaper. Longer adjectives usually use more: more comfortable. Use than to introduce the comparison. The cheapest identifies the lowest price in a group. Cheap enough means the price meets a need, not necessarily that it is the lowest.
reading: Maya needs a laptop for writing essays. Model A is cheaper than Model B, but its battery lasts only three hours. Model B lasts eight hours and is lighter. Maya often studies where there are no sockets. She chooses Model B even though it costs more. She does not need the fastest machine; she needs one that works all day.
comprehension: She needs to work away from sockets for much of the day.
The text explicitly describes Model B as lighter.
grammar: Complete the comparative: This bag is ___ (light) than that one.
lighter
Light takes -er.
Correct: This chair is more comfortabler than mine.
This chair is more comfortable than mine.
Use more comfortable, not a double comparative.
dialogue: Assistant: This model is the cheapest. You need to check its battery before deciding.
interaction: Choose the useful follow-up.
How long does the battery last?
Cheap means it is always best.
I do not use a laptop.
The question checks the feature relevant to the decision.
listening: The green backpack is twenty pounds. The red one is five pounds more, but it is waterproof. Both hold the same amount. I cycle in the rain, so I will buy the red one.
listening_questions: How much is the red backpack?
It costs five pounds more than twenty.
Why is the red one chosen?
Waterproofing matters when cycling in rain.

title: Health, advice and obligations
objective: Distinguish advice, rules and absence of obligation.
teaching: Should gives advice. Must or have to expresses an obligation. Must not prohibits an action; do not have to means it is optional. These meanings are different. Describe a symptom clearly, but seek professional advice for real health decisions.
reading: Ben has a sore throat and feels tired. He calls his clinic before going there. The receptionist says he should drink water and rest while he waits for his appointment. He must bring his identification card. He does not have to arrive an hour early; ten minutes is enough. The appointment is at eleven.
comprehension: Bringing identification is the stated requirement.
He does not have to arrive an hour early.
grammar: Complete with should or must not: For advice, say: You ___ rest.
should
Should signals advice, not a prohibition.
Replace must not with the correct phrase for no obligation: You ___ book in advance; walk-ins are welcome.
do not have to
No obligation is different from a ban on booking.
dialogue: Receptionist: We can see you at eleven or at three. You are working all afternoon and want the earlier appointment.
interaction: Choose a clear reply.
Eleven, please. I work in the afternoon.
Three is earlier than eleven.
I must not have an appointment.
The reply selects the appointment that fits the schedule.
listening: Your appointment is at ten forty on Monday. Please bring the letter we sent you. You do not need to fast. If you cannot attend, phone us before Friday.
listening_questions: The speaker explicitly says fasting is not needed.
When should a cancellation be reported?
The instruction is to phone before Friday.

title: Experiences and unfinished time
objective: Distinguish present-perfect experience from finished past events.
teaching: Use have or has plus a past participle for experience without a finished time: I have visited York. Use the past simple with yesterday or last year. Ever asks about experience; never says it has not happened. Been to usually describes a completed visit; gone to may mean the person is still away.
reading: Sofia has visited Scotland twice. Her first visit was in 2022, when she stayed in Edinburgh. This year she has travelled less because she is saving money. She has never been to Wales, but she hopes to go next spring. Her brother has gone to Cardiff for a course and will return on Friday.
comprehension: Which place has Sofia not visited?
She has never been to Wales.
What can we infer about her brother?
He is away on a course.
Has gone to Cardiff and will return on Friday indicate he is still away.
grammar: Complete: She has never ___ (be) to Wales.
been
Been is the past participle of be.
Correct the tense with a finished time: I have visited York yesterday.
I visited York yesterday.
Yesterday requires the past simple here.
dialogue: Friend: Have you ever been to Scotland? You went there once, last year.
interaction: Choose the appropriate answer.
Yes, I went there last year.
Yes, I go there yesterday.
No, I have gone there every Monday.
Answer the experience question and use past simple for last year.
listening: I have tried skiing, but only once. That was three years ago in France. I have not tried snowboarding yet. Next winter I want to take a beginner's lesson.
listening_questions: The speaker has tried skiing once.
Three years ago specifies the finished time.

title: Plans, predictions and invitations
objective: Discuss intentions and likely results using future forms and first conditionals.
teaching: Going to often describes an existing intention. Will can express a prediction or a decision made now. In a first conditional, use if plus present simple, then will plus base verb: If it rains, we will stay inside. An invitation should be accepted or declined clearly and politely.
reading: Our class is organising a picnic for Saturday. We are going to bring food to share. If it rains, we will meet in the community hall instead. The hall is already booked, so we will not need to cancel. Mina cannot come because she is visiting her grandparents. She offers to help prepare sandwiches on Friday.
comprehension: What will happen if it rains?
They will meet in the hall.
A booked indoor venue provides the alternative.
She cannot attend but offers help the previous day.
grammar: Complete: If it ___ (rain), we will use the hall.
rains
Use present simple in the if-clause.
Correct: If she will arrive early, we will start at ten.
If she arrives early, we will start at ten.
Do not use will in this ordinary first-conditional if-clause.
dialogue: Friend: Would you like to join our picnic? You cannot attend, but you want to thank them.
interaction: Choose a polite refusal.
Thanks for inviting me, but I cannot make it.
You must cancel the picnic.
No, nobody likes picnics.
The reply appreciates the invitation and states the limitation without attacking the event.
listening: We are going to leave at nine unless the bus is late. If it is late, I will send everyone a message. Please do not go straight to the park; meet at the school gate.
listening_questions: The speaker explicitly requests the school gate.
What will the speaker do if the bus is late?
A message will communicate the changed situation.

title: Narratives and turning points
objective: Connect background actions with completed events in a narrative.
teaching: The past continuous sets an action in progress; the past simple marks an event that interrupts it. The past perfect places an event before another past reference point. A clear narrative establishes context, identifies a turning point and explains the result. Do not infer a motive that the narrator does not provide.
reading: While Joel was walking home, he noticed an elderly neighbour standing outside her flat. She had locked herself out and had left her phone inside. Joel initially offered to call a locksmith. Then she remembered that her daughter kept a spare key. He lent her his phone, and her daughter arrived twenty minutes later. Joel was late for dinner, but the problem was solved without damaging the door.
comprehension: Had locked herself out places the event before his encounter.
Which action actually solved the problem?
Calling the daughter with a spare key
The daughter brought the spare key; a locksmith was only proposed.
grammar: Complete the background action: While he ___ (walk) home, he noticed her.
was walking
Past continuous supplies the ongoing background.
Use past perfect: She ___ (leave) her phone inside before he arrived.
had left
Had left marks the earlier of the two past events.
dialogue: Neighbour: I am sorry I made you late. You want to reassure her without pretending you had no other plans.
interaction: Choose the balanced reply.
You always cause trouble.
I am glad we sorted it out; I can let my family know.
Nothing happened and nobody helped.
The reply acknowledges the solution and manages the delay constructively.
listening: I was waiting for a delivery when the fire alarm rang. I left the building immediately. The parcel arrived while we were outside, so the driver took it back to the depot.
listening_questions: The driver took it back because the recipient was outside.

title: Learning strategies and advice
objective: Explain problems, recommend strategies and discuss hypothetical choices.
teaching: A second conditional imagines a situation: If I had more time, I would practise daily. Unlike a first conditional, it does not present the condition as a straightforward expectation. Advice should respond to the actual difficulty. Separate a strategy's purpose from a guaranteed result.
reading: Priya can understand articles when she reads slowly, but she forgets new words during conversation. Her tutor suggests keeping a small notebook with phrases rather than isolated translations. Priya also records a short summary after reading and listens to it the next day. The tutor does not promise instant fluency. The aim is to practise retrieving useful language regularly, not to memorise every unfamiliar word.
comprehension: She understands slow reading but struggles with retrieval in conversation.
Recording useful phrases and practising retrieval
The notebook and summaries support repeated retrieval, not exhaustive memorisation.
grammar: Complete: If I had more time, I ___ practise every day.
would
A hypothetical second conditional uses would in its result clause.
Complete: If she ___ (be) more confident, she would speak more. Use the formal hypothetical form.
were
Were is the formal hypothetical form with all subjects.
dialogue: Classmate: I study long lists, but I cannot use the words when speaking. You want to suggest a manageable alternative.
interaction: Choose targeted advice.
You should never study vocabulary.
Why not practise a few useful phrases in short conversations?
Buy a larger dictionary and stop speaking.
The suggestion addresses active retrieval with a realistic task.
listening: I used to highlight almost every sentence. Now I read a section, close the book and explain the main point aloud. It takes longer at first, but I notice gaps in my understanding much sooner.
listening_questions: What changed in the study method?
Explaining without looking at the book
The new method involves retrieval and explanation.
What benefit does the speaker report?
The reported benefit is detecting gaps, not guaranteed perfect memory.

title: Work and practical communication
objective: Report requests, clarify responsibilities and use common passive forms.
teaching: The passive focuses on an action or recipient: the form is checked every morning. Use be plus past participle. Reported requests can use asked someone to do something. In practical messages, state the task, deadline and responsible person; ask for clarification rather than assume.
reading: At a small design studio, customer requests are entered into a shared system. Each morning, Lena checks new requests and assigns urgent ones to a designer. Yesterday, a client asked the team to change a delivery address. Lena updated the record but did not tell the courier. The team now sends a separate confirmation whenever an address changes, because updating the system alone did not reach everyone involved.
comprehension: The shared system had no records.
A record update did not inform the courier.
The communication gap was between the system update and the courier.
A separate confirmation for address changes
The team adds confirmation rather than abandoning the system.
grammar: Change to passive: The team checks the form. Begin: The form...
The form is checked by the team.
Present-simple passive uses is checked; retain the agent as requested.
Complete the reported request: The client asked us ___ change the address.
to
Ask someone to do something reports a request.
dialogue: Manager: Please finish this soon. You have two urgent tasks and need a precise priority and deadline.
interaction: Which clarification is most useful?
Soon means whenever I want.
Should I prioritise this over the report, and when do you need it?
You never give good instructions.
The question clarifies both priority and timing without blame.
listening: Please send the draft to me by Thursday noon, not directly to the client. I will check the figures, and then you can email the approved version on Friday.
listening_questions: The draft goes to the speaker for checking.
When can the approved version be sent?
Friday follows the check of the draft.

title: Community and consequences
objective: Explain social proposals using reasons, results and relative clauses.
teaching: Use who for people and which for things in defining relative clauses. Because introduces a reason; so introduces a result. A proposal can have benefits and costs at the same time. When summarising a local issue, identify who is affected and distinguish the proposal from an agreed decision.
reading: Residents have proposed turning an unused car park into a community garden. People who live in nearby flats would gain a place to grow vegetables. However, a local shop uses the car park for deliveries twice a week. The council has not made a decision. It has invited residents and shop owners to discuss a design that keeps a small delivery area while creating space for planting.
comprehension: What is the council's current position?
It has already built the garden.
The council has invited discussion and has not decided.
Keeping a delivery area alongside planting space
The design attempts to meet both groups' needs.
grammar: Complete: Residents ___ live nearby can join. Use who or which.
who
Who introduces a defining clause about people.
Join using because: The shop needs access. It receives deliveries. Begin: The shop needs access...
The shop needs access because it receives deliveries.
Because introduces the reason for needing access.
dialogue: At a meeting, someone says: Anyone who questions the garden is against the community. You support the garden but recognise delivery needs.
interaction: Choose a constructive response.
There are no practical problems.
We can support the garden and still discuss access for deliveries.
All shops should close immediately.
The reply rejects a false either-or choice and focuses on a workable concern.
listening: The library will extend its evening hours for a three-month trial. Volunteers will help with events, but paid staff will still manage borrowing. After the trial, the council will review attendance before deciding whether to continue.
listening_questions: Paid staff retain responsibility for borrowing.
Not yet; attendance will be reviewed
The three-month trial precedes a decision.

title: News, claims and sources
objective: Distinguish a reported claim from verified information.
teaching: Reported speech often shifts present to past when reporting from a later viewpoint. Said is followed by a clause; told normally needs an object. A headline may state a claim more strongly than the article supports. Check who supplied a figure, when it was measured and whether another source confirms it.
reading: A headline claimed that a town had stopped using plastic bags. The article explained that three supermarkets had removed free bags, but smaller shops could still sell them. A campaign group said the change would reduce waste. The council had not yet measured the effect. Mia shared the article with a note explaining the limited scope, rather than repeating the headline as if it described every shop.
comprehension: Only three supermarkets changed their practice; the headline implied the whole town.
The council had not yet measured the effect.
grammar: Report yesterday's words using backshift: She said, 'I am tired.' Begin: She said that...
She said that she was tired.
Am becomes was in the requested backshift.
Complete with said or told: He ___ me that the shop was closed.
told
Told takes the object me.
dialogue: Friend: This headline proves every shop has banned bags. You have read the full article and want to correct the claim politely.
interaction: Choose the accurate correction.
The article only describes three supermarkets, so the headline is broader than the evidence.
Every headline is always false.
There is no way to check any claim.
The response identifies the specific mismatch without dismissing all reporting.
listening: The survey found that sixty percent of respondents preferred the new timetable. However, only eighty people replied, and most were regular commuters. We should not assume that the results represent every resident.
listening_questions: Eighty respondents, mostly commuters, may not represent all residents.
What does sixty percent refer to?
The percentage describes respondents, not the entire population.

title: Decisions and possible outcomes
objective: Discuss alternatives, hypothetical outcomes and practical trade-offs.
teaching: First conditionals discuss plausible future conditions; second conditionals imagine less direct or unreal situations. Might expresses possibility, not certainty. A trade-off means gaining one benefit while accepting a cost. Recommend an option in relation to stated needs rather than assuming one choice is best for everyone.
reading: Rafael has been offered a job in another city. The salary is higher, but rent would also cost more. His current job is close to his family and allows flexible hours. He asks the new employer whether he could work remotely two days a week. If the employer agrees, he will accept. If he had no family responsibilities, he would be more willing to move immediately.
comprehension: He will accept if the employer agrees to two remote days.
Why is the higher salary not enough by itself?
Rent and family responsibilities also matter.
The decision includes financial costs and family needs.
grammar: Complete: If they agree, I ___ accept. Use will or would.
will
The first conditional presents a real future possibility.
Complete: If I had fewer responsibilities, I ___ move. Use will or would.
would
The second conditional imagines a different present situation.
dialogue: Recruiter: The salary is higher, so surely you can accept today. You want to discuss an important condition first.
interaction: Choose a professional reply.
Salary is the only thing that matters.
I appreciate the offer. Could we clarify the remote-working arrangement before I decide?
There is nothing to discuss.
The response acknowledges the offer while requesting necessary information.
listening: I chose the evening course because I could keep my job. It means travelling home late twice a week, which is tiring. If the college offers a weekend group next term, I will consider switching.
listening_questions: The evening course allows continued employment.
The speaker finds the late journeys tiring.

title: Developing a balanced argument
objective: Evaluate competing arguments, concessions and qualified conclusions.
teaching: A balanced argument concedes a reasonable opposing point before explaining its limits. Although introduces a concession, whereas contrasts alternatives. Avoid changing may into will when summarising a claim. A conclusion should reflect the strength and scope of the evidence, not just repeat the most forceful opinion.
reading: A university is considering recording all lectures. Supporters argue that recordings help students who are ill or need to revisit difficult material. Critics worry that attendance could decline and discussion could become less spontaneous. A pilot found no overall fall in attendance, although participation varied by subject. The report recommends offering recordings alongside in-person teaching rather than treating them as a replacement. It also notes that a one-term pilot cannot establish every long-term effect.
comprehension: Use recordings as a supplement while monitoring effects.
The report supports supplementation and qualifies the pilot's scope.
What does the pilot fail to establish?
A single term does not establish all long-term outcomes.
grammar: Combine using although: Attendance remained stable. Participation varied. Begin: Although participation...
Although participation varied, attendance remained stable.
Although concedes variation while preserving the main finding.
Complete: Some students prefer recordings, ___ others value live discussion. Use whereas or because.
whereas
Whereas contrasts preferences rather than stating a cause.
dialogue: Colleague: The pilot proves recordings can never harm attendance. You want to preserve the finding without overstating it.
interaction: Choose the best qualification.
The pilot found no overall decline, but that does not settle every long-term question.
The pilot contains no information at all.
Attendance must always fall.
The reply retains the finding while limiting the inference.
listening: I support the proposal in principle. What worries me is the assumption that one format will suit every department. Let us keep the common goal but allow departments to test different approaches before adopting a single policy.
listening_questions: Support in principle is paired with a concern about uniform implementation.
The speaker favours local trials before a uniform policy.

title: Evidence, likelihood and causation
objective: Interpret uncertainty and distinguish association from causation.
teaching: May, might and could signal possibility; must can express a strong deduction, not only obligation. An association does not by itself establish that one factor caused another. Compare groups, alternative explanations and limits of measurement. Use appears to and suggests when stronger certainty would exceed the evidence.
reading: An article reported that employees who cycled to work took fewer sick days. The study followed volunteers rather than randomly assigning commuting methods. Cyclists may have differed in health or working patterns before the study began. The researchers described an association and called for further investigation. A company newsletter nevertheless announced that buying a bicycle would prevent illness. That claim turns a group-level observation into an individual guarantee the research did not provide.
comprehension: Why is the newsletter's conclusion too strong?
It promises causation and certainty not established by the study.
The study did not involve employees.
An observational association cannot justify an individual guarantee.
Cyclists may already have differed in health.
Pre-existing differences could contribute to the association.
grammar: Complete with may or must: The evidence is limited; the difference ___ reflect prior health.
may
May expresses a possible explanation without certainty.
Use a perfect modal deduction: The office is dark and empty. They ___ (leave). Use must.
must have left
Must have plus past participle expresses a strong deduction about the past.
dialogue: Editor: Can we write that cycling prevents illness? You have only the observational study described above.
interaction: Choose a responsible recommendation.
Say the study found an association, and explain its limits.
Guarantee that no cyclist becomes ill.
Remove all mention of the study's design.
The recommendation preserves the finding without inventing causal certainty.
listening: Sales rose after the redesign, but the launch coincided with a major discount campaign. We cannot attribute the entire increase to the new website. A comparison period without discounts would help us separate the effects.
listening_questions: A discount campaign occurred at the same time.
The concurrent campaign is a competing explanation.
The comparison could help separate the redesign from the discount effect.

title: Negotiating workable agreements
objective: Express conditions, concessions and boundaries in a negotiation.
teaching: Provided that and as long as introduce conditions. Would be willing to expresses a conditional offer, not an existing agreement. A concession gives something up to obtain something else. Distinguish a non-negotiable constraint from a preference, and confirm the final terms rather than assuming silence means acceptance.
reading: A supplier can deliver equipment two weeks earlier if the buyer accepts a smaller first shipment. The buyer needs at least forty units for a launch but can wait for the remaining sixty. The supplier initially offers thirty units. After checking stock, it agrees to forty, provided that the buyer confirms by noon. The buyer asks for the revised dates and quantities in writing before signing. Neither side gets its original ideal, but both protect their main operational need.
comprehension: What is the buyer's essential requirement?
At least forty units for launch
Forty units are needed for launch; sixty may arrive later.
The buyer requests written dates and quantities.
grammar: Complete with provided that or despite: We can deliver early ___ you confirm today.
provided that
Provided that introduces the condition for early delivery.
Correct: We would willing to accept a partial shipment.
We would be willing to accept a partial shipment.
The conditional expression needs be before willing.
dialogue: Supplier: We can offer thirty now. Buyer: We need forty for launch. You want to move the negotiation forward without abandoning that minimum.
interaction: Choose the constructive counteroffer.
Thirty is fine even though the launch needs forty.
If you can provide forty now, we can accept the remaining sixty later.
There is no possible solution.
The offer preserves the minimum while conceding on the rest of the delivery.
listening: We could extend the contract for a year, provided the support response time is reduced to four hours. The price can remain unchanged. Without that service commitment, we would prefer a shorter extension.
listening_questions: What condition is attached to a year-long extension?
The service response time is the stated condition.
The speaker prefers a shorter extension if the condition is not met.

title: Reporting events and perspectives
objective: Use reported speech and passive structures while preserving attribution.
teaching: Report what a source says without silently endorsing it. It is alleged that signals an allegation, not a proven fact. The passive can foreground an event when the agent is unknown or unimportant, but should not conceal responsibility where it matters. Preserve qualifications and differences between sources.
reading: After a service outage, the operator said that a software update had triggered unexpected errors. An independent review found that testing had not covered a common usage pattern. Customers criticised the delay in communication, rather than the update alone. The final report recommended both broader testing and clearer incident notices. A summary that blamed only individual programmers would omit the review's focus on process and communication.
comprehension: What did the independent review identify?
The review found a gap in test coverage.
What would a programmer-only explanation miss?
The report recommends systemic improvements, not only individual blame.
grammar: Report with backshift: The operator said, 'We are investigating.' Begin: The operator said that...
The operator said that they were investigating.
The requested report shifts are investigating to were investigating and we to they.
Change to passive, retaining the agent: The review identified two failures. Begin: Two failures...
Two failures were identified by the review.
Past-simple passive uses were identified.
dialogue: A colleague writes: The operator proved the update was the only cause. The source merely says the operator reported a trigger, while a review found wider issues.
interaction: Choose the accurate revision.
Attribute the operator's account and include the review's wider findings.
Present the operator's statement as independent proof.
Delete the review because it complicates the story.
Attribution and the wider findings prevent a misleading single-cause account.
listening: The chair said the decision had been postponed, not rejected. Members wanted more detail about costs. A revised proposal is expected next month, but no date for a final vote has been announced.
listening_questions: Postponed is explicitly contrasted with rejected.
The date of the final vote
No final voting date has been announced.

title: Environment and policy trade-offs
objective: Evaluate policy choices using conditions, counterfactuals and impacts.
teaching: Third conditionals consider a different past: If they had invested earlier, costs would have fallen. They do not describe what actually happened. Policy arguments should identify distributional effects: an overall benefit can coexist with costs for a particular group. Distinguish a target, a forecast and an observed outcome.
reading: A city introduced charges for high-emission vehicles in its centre. Air quality improved during the first year, but small delivery firms reported higher replacement costs. The council offered grants, although applicants criticised a slow process. An evaluation recommended keeping the charge while simplifying grants and improving alternatives for deliveries. It did not conclude that the policy had no costs, nor that every improvement in air quality could be attributed to the charge alone.
comprehension: Retain it while improving support and alternatives.
The recommendation combines retention with mitigation of practical burdens.
The charge alone caused all air-quality improvement.
The text does not attribute every improvement solely to the charge.
grammar: Complete the third conditional: If they had invested earlier, costs ___ (fall). Use would.
would have fallen
A past counterfactual result uses would have plus past participle.
Complete: If the grants ___ (arrive) sooner, firms would have replaced vehicles. Use past perfect.
had arrived
Past perfect supplies the unreal past condition.
dialogue: At a consultation, someone says: Since air improved, we should ignore delivery firms' concerns. You want to acknowledge both effects.
interaction: Choose a balanced reply.
An overall benefit does not remove the need to address uneven costs.
Any cost proves there was no benefit.
No evaluation is necessary.
The reply distinguishes total benefits from their distribution.
listening: The scheme aims to cut energy demand by ten percent. That is a target, not a measured result. Early readings cover only the summer months, so we need winter data before judging annual savings.
listening_questions: The speaker explicitly labels it as a target.

title: Culture, interpretation and reviews
objective: Interpret evaluative language and distinguish taste from reasoned judgement.
teaching: A review combines description, evaluation and reasons. An unfamiliar style is not automatically a flaw. Comparisons should identify the criterion used. Not only... but also links parallel elements. A mixed review can praise one aspect while criticising another; do not reduce it to simply positive or negative.
reading: The exhibition places everyday objects beside recordings of their owners' memories. One reviewer praises its intimate scale but finds the written labels too vague to explain the historical setting. Another welcomes that openness, arguing that visitors should form their own connections. Both admire the sound design. Their disagreement concerns how much interpretive guidance a museum should provide, rather than whether the objects are valuable or whether the recordings are technically effective.
comprehension: The reviewers differ over interpretive guidance, while agreeing on sound design.
The shared positive judgement concerns sound design.
grammar: Complete the parallel structure: The show is not only intimate ___ also thought-provoking.
but
Not only pairs with but also.
Combine with whereas: One reviewer wants more guidance. The other values openness. Begin: One reviewer wants more guidance...
One reviewer wants more guidance, whereas the other values openness.
Whereas makes the contrast explicit.
dialogue: Friend: If the labels do not explain everything, the exhibition must be bad. You want to invite a more precise judgement.
interaction: Choose the nuanced response.
Could we separate the quality of the work from our preference for more guidance?
Every exhibition is equally good.
Visitors should never ask questions.
The response distinguishes a criterion or preference from a total verdict.
listening: The novel's opening is slow, and I nearly stopped reading. Yet the restrained pace makes the final revelation convincing. I would recommend it to readers who enjoy gradual character development, rather than those looking for constant action.
listening_questions: How does the reviewer assess the slow pace?
As initially difficult but ultimately useful
The pace initially discourages the reviewer but supports the ending.
The recommendation is explicitly qualified by reader preference.

title: Stance, hedging and calibrated claims
objective: Express degrees of commitment and identify overstatement in complex argument.
teaching: Advanced argument calibrates commitment. The evidence is consistent with is weaker than the evidence establishes. Hedging is not evasiveness when it accurately reflects uncertainty. Fronted negative adverbials can trigger inversion: Rarely have we seen. Evaluate what a qualification limits: the population, the mechanism, the timescale or the certainty of the claim.
reading: The committee's report cautiously endorses flexible working, noting improvements in retention across several participating firms. It stops short of attributing those improvements solely to location flexibility: the firms also changed management practices. Critics interpret the qualification as a lack of confidence in flexible work itself. Yet the report's position is narrower. It supports continued adoption where appropriate while resisting a universal causal claim. Its caution concerns the explanation and generalisability of the findings, not the existence of the observed retention changes.
comprehension: What is the qualification primarily about?
Whether retention was observed at all
The report accepts the observations but limits causal and universal interpretations.
How do critics misread the report?
They equate a limited causal claim with rejection of flexible work.
They note that several firms participated.
They turn methodological caution into broad opposition or doubt.
grammar: Rewrite with inversion, starting Rarely: We have rarely seen such consistent findings.
Rarely have we seen such consistent findings.
Fronted rarely requires subject-auxiliary inversion.
Complete: The findings are consistent ___ this explanation, but do not establish it.
with
Consistent with expresses compatibility rather than proof.
dialogue: A colleague wants to replace 'may contribute to retention' with 'guarantees retention' in the report summary.
interaction: Which objection is precise?
The revision changes a possible contribution into an unsupported guarantee.
All confident writing is dishonest.
The original phrase has no meaning.
The objection identifies the exact change in evidential commitment.
listening: I would not dismiss the pattern, but neither would I build a universal rule on it. The sample is unusually stable, and that may be why the intervention appears so effective. Replication in less predictable settings would strengthen the case.
listening_questions: Accepting a pattern while limiting generalisation
The speaker neither dismisses nor universalises the pattern.
Replication would test whether the effect extends beyond the stable sample.

title: Register and diplomatic disagreement
objective: Adjust directness and register while preserving a substantive objection.
teaching: Diplomatic language can reduce interpersonal friction without weakening a clear boundary. I am not persuaded that challenges an inference; with respect may sound confrontational if followed by dismissal. Match register to audience, power relationship and purpose. Formal concessive structures such as while and notwithstanding organise disagreement without pretending agreement.
reading: During a partnership meeting, the project lead says, 'The timetable is ambitious.' The supplier takes this as praise and confirms the launch date. In a follow-up message, the lead writes that the team cannot commit until testing is complete. The initial remark was intended as a reservation, but its indirectness left the practical consequence unstated. The revised message remains courteous while naming the dependency, the risk of premature launch and the earliest point at which a reliable date can be agreed.
comprehension: Why did the initial communication fail?
It named the testing dependency too clearly.
The reservation was indirect and its consequence unstated.
Ambitious was interpreted positively because the intended reservation was not explicit.
A courteous but explicit condition for commitment
The follow-up connects the concern to testing and the date decision.
grammar: Complete the formal concession: ___ we appreciate the urgency, testing must be completed. Use While or Because.
While
While concedes the urgency without making it the reason to skip testing.
Rewrite more formally with the supplied words: We cannot agree yet. Begin: We are not yet in a position...
We are not yet in a position to agree.
In a position to expresses present capacity in a formal register.
dialogue: A senior colleague proposes publishing unverified figures today. You need to disagree respectfully and make the constraint explicit.
interaction: Choose the effective reply.
Interesting. I am sure it will be fine.
I appreciate the deadline, but I cannot approve publication until the figures are verified.
Your proposal is ridiculous.
The reply combines acknowledgement, a clear boundary and its condition.
listening: The draft is certainly comprehensive. My concern is not the amount of material but whether a non-specialist can locate the decision we need them to make. A shorter executive summary might do more than adding another appendix.
listening_questions: The concern is finding the decision, not document length alone.
Acknowledges a strength before a reservation
It concedes breadth before introducing a functional criticism.

title: Synthesising sources without flattening them
objective: Combine perspectives while preserving disagreements and evidential limits.
teaching: Synthesis organises sources around an issue, not just one source after another. Preserve differences in scope and method. Both texts agree that does not mean they share a solution. Nominalisation can compress an idea, but excessive abstraction hides agents and processes. Identify which apparent contradictions disappear when definitions or populations are distinguished.
reading: One study finds that remote employees report fewer interruptions; another finds that new recruits learn workplace routines more slowly when fully remote. These findings need not conflict. The first concerns established staff's concentration, whereas the second concerns newcomers' informal learning. A synthesis that simply labels remote work beneficial or harmful erases this distinction. A more useful account asks which tasks and career stages benefit from which arrangements, while acknowledging that self-reports and observed induction outcomes measure different things.
comprehension: Why need the findings not conflict?
They concern different groups and outcomes.
Established staff's interruptions and newcomers' learning are different outcomes.
Its effects may depend on task and career stage.
Both sources prove the same mechanism.
The proposed synthesis retains conditions and differences between methods.
grammar: Nominalise improve in this sentence: The ___ of induction procedures is a priority.
improvement
Improvement names the process as a noun.
Complete the contrast: The first study concerns concentration, ___ the second concerns induction. Use whereas.
whereas
Whereas links the contrasting scopes.
dialogue: An editor asks you to compress both studies into: 'Experts disagree about whether remote work works.' You want to preserve the meaningful distinction.
interaction: Choose the better summary.
The studies examine different outcomes, suggesting arrangements should reflect staff experience and tasks.
Experts can never agree on anything.
The two studies cancel each other out.
The summary relates the findings without inventing a direct contradiction.
listening: Both authors favour wider access, but they mean different things by access. One counts enrolments; the other examines whether students can participate meaningfully once enrolled. A rise in the first measure does not settle the second question.
listening_questions: Where does the apparent agreement conceal a difference?
The same word refers to entry in one account and meaningful participation in another.
What can increased enrolment establish by itself?
More entries, not necessarily meaningful participation
The first measure cannot by itself answer the second question.

title: Implication and institutional language
objective: Infer pragmatic meaning without treating an inference as explicit fact.
teaching: An implication is suggested rather than stated. Inferences depend on context and remain revisable. Institutional language may distribute or obscure responsibility through passive voice, agentless nominalisations and vague references. Ask what is explicitly committed to, what is merely envisaged and who can be held responsible for the next step.
reading: The announcement states that 'implementation difficulties were encountered' and that 'lessons will inform future practice'. It identifies neither the decisions that created the difficulties nor the person responsible for acting on the lessons. Readers might reasonably infer an attempt to avoid blame, but that motive is not established by the wording alone. What can be demonstrated is the absence of named accountability, a timetable and a measurable commitment. A careful critique distinguishes those textual features from speculation about the authors' intentions.
comprehension: Which claim is demonstrable from the wording?
Named accountability and a timetable are absent.
Those omissions are observable; motives are not established.
What distinction does the passage insist on?
Textual evidence versus speculation about intention
A plausible motive remains an inference rather than an explicit fact.
grammar: Make responsibility explicit: A review will be conducted by the board. Begin: The board...
The board will conduct a review.
Active voice names the board as the responsible agent.
Complete: The wording gives rise ___ concerns about accountability.
to
Give rise to means cause or generate.
dialogue: Colleague: The vague announcement proves the authors wanted to deceive us. You want to criticise the text without overstating knowledge of motive.
interaction: Choose the careful response.
We can show that accountability is unspecified; deliberate deception would require further evidence.
There is nothing to criticise.
Vagueness always proves fraud.
The reply separates observable omission from an unsupported intentional claim.
listening: We envisage a review in due course. That is not a promise to publish one by the end of the year. If a publication deadline is essential to the agreement, it needs to be specified rather than inferred from this statement.
listening_questions: What commitment has actually been made?
Envisage and in due course do not fix a publication date.
What should be added if timing matters?
An explicit deadline avoids relying on inference.

title: Evaluation and counterarguments
objective: Assess a counterargument and distinguish necessary from sufficient conditions.
teaching: A necessary condition must hold for an outcome, but may not guarantee it. A sufficient condition is enough to produce the outcome under stated assumptions. A counterexample can refute a universal claim without proving the opposite universal claim. Address the strongest relevant objection, not an easier caricature of it.
reading: A funding proposal argues that public data access will automatically improve research quality. A reviewer agrees that access removes a barrier but notes that data also need usable documentation, appropriate methods and ethical safeguards. This is not an argument against openness. It challenges the claim that openness alone is sufficient. Pointing to one poorly documented open dataset would undermine an automatic guarantee, but would not establish that closed datasets are generally better. The revised proposal makes access one component of a broader quality strategy.
comprehension: The reviewer accepts a benefit while rejecting an automatic guarantee.
What would one poor open dataset establish?
That all closed data are better
A counterexample to the automatic guarantee
A counterexample defeats a universal guarantee, not every weaker benefit claim.
grammar: Complete: Access is necessary but not ___ for quality. Use sufficient.
sufficient
Necessary does not entail sufficient.
Rewrite using by no means and inversion: This is not a complete solution. Begin: By no means...
By no means is this a complete solution.
A fronted negative phrase triggers inversion.
dialogue: Presenter: You questioned whether access guarantees quality, so you must oppose access. You want to correct the characterisation.
interaction: Choose the precise reply.
I support access; my objection is to treating it as sufficient on its own.
Yes, no data should ever be shared.
Quality cannot be discussed.
The reply separates support for a component from acceptance of a guarantee.
listening: The objection is not that the proposal can never work. It is that success depends on staffing levels the budget does not provide. Unless that dependency is addressed, the projected savings remain conditional rather than assured.
listening_questions: The staffing dependency is missing from the budget.
How should the savings be described?
The speaker explicitly calls them conditional.

title: Mediating technical information
objective: Reformulate specialist information for a non-specialist without losing conditions.
teaching: Mediation is not word-for-word replacement. Identify the audience's decision, retain the conditions that affect it and explain essential terms. Omit incidental detail rather than material uncertainty. In mixed conditionals, an unreal past cause can have a present result: If we had checked, we would know now.
reading: A technical note says a monitoring device estimates average exposure over a day, not the maximum concentration at every instant. A school administrator asks whether one low daily reading proves there were no short peaks. An accurate plain-language explanation must say no: an average can conceal brief higher values. It should not imply the device is useless, because daily exposure remains relevant to a different question. The recommendation is to match the measurement method to the decision, and use time-resolved data when short peaks matter.
comprehension: What does the low daily average fail to rule out?
The existence of a whole day
An average does not identify every momentary peak.
Choose data suited to the decision
The daily average and time-resolved data answer different questions.
grammar: Complete the mixed conditional: If we had measured the peaks, we ___ know more now. Use would.
would
Would plus base form gives the present result of a counterfactual past.
Complete: The method should be suited ___ the question being asked.
to
Suited to expresses fitness for a purpose.
dialogue: Administrator: Can I tell parents that the low average means there were no peaks? You must give a clear, non-alarmist explanation.
interaction: Choose the accurate reformulation.
No. The average describes the whole day; brief peaks require more detailed measurements.
Yes. An average is always the maximum.
No measurement can tell us anything.
The reply preserves the limitation without dismissing all measurement.
listening: The model gives a range, not an appointment with the future. For planning, use the range to test whether your decision remains workable under several plausible outcomes. Do not turn the middle estimate into a promise the model never made.
listening_questions: A forecast as an exact future appointment
The metaphor highlights the mistaken demand for a precise guarantee.
How should the range be used?
The speaker recommends robustness across the range.

title: Rhetorical framing and presupposition
objective: Analyse how framing invites acceptance of an unestablished premise.
teaching: A loaded question can presuppose the very proposition under dispute. Asking when a policy's benefits will finally be acknowledged presupposes benefits and a failure to acknowledge them. Distinguish grammatical presupposition, contextual implication and independently warranted conclusions. Rejecting a loaded premise does not require asserting its opposite.
reading: The editorial asks when the city will 'finally admit' that its experiment has failed. The phrasing presents failure as settled and casts disagreement as reluctance to confess. Yet the evidence described is mixed: one target was missed, another was exceeded, and the principal outcome has not been measured. A response that merely answers 'next year' accepts the frame. A more discriminating response first questions the criterion of failure, then evaluates each outcome separately. This does not vindicate the experiment; it prevents a rhetorical premise from doing the work of an argument.
comprehension: What does 'finally admit' invite the reader to accept?
Admit frames failure as a truth awaiting reluctant recognition.
What would questioning the frame establish by itself?
The failure claim still needs an argued criterion.
Challenging a premise does not prove the opposite conclusion.
grammar: Rewrite with emphatic what-cleft: We need an explicit criterion. Begin: What we need...
What we need is an explicit criterion.
The what-cleft foregrounds the missing criterion.
Complete the correlative: The issue is not ___ the policy is popular, but whether it meets its stated aims.
whether
Not whether... but whether contrasts the questions under consideration.
dialogue: Interviewer: When will you finally concede that the trial was a disaster? You need to resist the premise without avoiding evaluation.
interaction: Choose the rigorous response.
Next Tuesday.
Let us specify the criteria: some targets were missed, others met, and the main outcome is unmeasured.
All criticism is illegitimate.
The reply replaces the presupposition with differentiated evaluation.
listening: Calling the measure a rescue rather than a subsidy does not change its cost, but it changes the story about who deserves it. My objection is not to the payment itself; it is to allowing that label to substitute for an account of its purpose and effects.
listening_questions: The arithmetic of a stated cost
The objection concerns rhetorical framing doing the work of justification.
What contrast does the label create?
A new recipient by legal definition
The speaker emphasises the label's narrative effect, not a change in cost.

title: Irony, understatement and perspective
objective: Infer irony from context while keeping literal and intended meanings distinct.
teaching: Irony often creates a gap between literal praise and contextual criticism. Understatement deliberately expresses less than the situation warrants. Neither can be identified from a word alone: context, shared assumptions and delivery matter. Explain what evidence supports an ironic reading, and acknowledge alternatives when delivery or context is unavailable.
reading: After the committee's third meeting about arranging a meeting, Lina remarked that their efficiency was 'a model for the ages'. The narrator adds that no agenda had yet been agreed. The extravagant praise clashes with the procedural stagnation, supporting an ironic reading. Another member's later comment, 'We may be slightly behind', is an understatement of the same delay. Neither remark supplies a plan. The passage exposes institutional inertia through the distance between how progress is described and what has actually been accomplished, rather than through a direct accusation of incompetence.
comprehension: What supports the ironic reading of Lina's remark?
The mismatch between extravagant praise and lack of progress
Contextual stagnation conflicts with the apparent praise.
As understatement of a substantial delay
The mild expression downplays the delay already established.
grammar: Rewrite with such...that: Their delay was so great that the launch was missed. Begin: Such was...
Such was their delay that the launch was missed.
Such was fronting creates an emphatic result construction.
Complete: The praise is at odds ___ the events described.
with
At odds with expresses conflict or inconsistency.
dialogue: A colleague quotes 'a model for the ages' as sincere approval, omitting the repeated meetings and absent agenda.
interaction: Choose the context-sensitive correction.
The surrounding lack of progress makes the apparent praise ironic, not straightforward endorsement.
Any extravagant phrase is always ironic.
Literal meanings never matter.
The correction grounds its interpretation in contextual evidence.
listening: Well, that was a wonderfully decisive afternoon: three hours, four revised minutes, and not a single decision. I suppose we can at least congratulate ourselves on having postponed the next postponement.
listening_questions: Literal praise of a final decision
The absence of any decision contradicts the literal praise.
A claim that the meeting was brief
Postponing a postponement extends the joke about procedural inertia.

title: Ambiguity and scope
objective: Resolve syntactic and pragmatic ambiguity without inventing certainty.
teaching: Scope determines what a negation, quantifier or modifier applies to. Not all is not equivalent to none. Only can focus on different elements depending on position and context. When an ambiguous phrase affects a decision, reformulate each reading and request clarification instead of silently choosing the convenient one.
reading: A contract summary says that the provider will not replace all damaged components. One manager reads this as a refusal to replace any; another assumes that every essential component is covered. Neither conclusion follows from the sentence alone. 'Not all' excludes universal coverage but does not identify the covered subset or guarantee that it is non-empty in this context. The operative schedule must specify the components and conditions. The ambiguity is practically important: fluent paraphrase can make an interpretation sound settled even when the underlying entitlement remains unspecified.
comprehension: What does the summary clearly exclude?
Not all denies all-inclusive coverage without specifying the actual covered subset.
What is needed to resolve the practical issue?
A schedule naming components and conditions
A repetition of the same ambiguous sentence
An explicit operative schedule establishes the entitlement.
grammar: Complete the distinction: Not all is not equivalent ___ none.
to
Equivalent to expresses sameness of meaning; these expressions differ in scope.
Place only before the subject to focus on the person: Maya approved the draft. Begin: Only...
Only Maya approved the draft.
Only before Maya excludes other approvers, not other objects of approval.
dialogue: Manager: It says 'not all', so we can tell clients that none will be replaced. You want to stop an unjustified paraphrase.
interaction: Choose the precise intervention.
That changes the scope; we need the coverage schedule before stating which components are excluded.
Yes, not all always means none.
Every essential component must be covered.
The response identifies the scope shift and seeks the governing detail.
listening: I said we had not approved every recommendation. I did not say we had rejected the report as a whole. Several recommendations are approved; two require clarification, and one is outside our remit.
listening_questions: The speaker corrects a universal negative reading of partial non-approval.
Why is one recommendation not being handled?
The speaker says one falls outside their responsibility.

title: Lexical precision and evaluative force
objective: Select near-synonyms according to implication, collocation and evidential force.
teaching: Near-synonyms differ in commitment and evaluation. Concede suggests reluctant acceptance; acknowledge need not imply reluctance. Refute claims to disprove, whereas rebut can mean offering a counterargument. Plausible is not synonymous with proven. Precision requires preserving these distinctions, especially when compressing another person's position.
reading: A commentary says the researcher 'conceded' that the data were incomplete and that a later response 'refuted' her explanation. The interview, however, shows her identifying the limitation at the outset, not yielding it under pressure. The response proposes an alternative mechanism but provides no decisive test between the two accounts. 'Acknowledged' and 'challenged' would therefore be more defensible choices. The original wording does not merely add colour: it recasts open methodological caution as retreat and unresolved disagreement as settled defeat.
comprehension: The limitation was volunteered, not reluctantly yielded.
The interview provides no evidence of the reluctance or reversal suggested by conceded.
There is no decisive discrimination between mechanisms.
Any response proves an explanation false.
A counterproposal without a decisive test does not establish disproof.
grammar: Complete the collocation: The evidence falls short ___ establishing causation.
of
Fall short of means fail to reach the required standard.
Use the requested reporting verb in past simple: She ___ (acknowledge) the limitation at the outset.
acknowledged
Acknowledged reports recognition without necessarily implying reluctant concession.
dialogue: Editor: 'Destroyed the argument' is punchier than 'raised an unresolved objection'. The evidence supports only the latter.
interaction: Choose the principled response.
Keep the stronger phrase because vividness overrides accuracy.
The punchier wording would turn an unresolved challenge into an unsupported claim of defeat.
Remove every evaluative verb from English.
The response explains the change in epistemic force rather than objecting to style generally.
listening: The findings warrant concern, not panic. They are compatible with the proposed mechanism, not uniquely explained by it. If those distinctions sound cautious, that is because the evidence requires caution, not because the question is unimportant.
listening_questions: That the mechanism is the unique explanation
Why does the speaker use cautious language?
Caution is justified by evidential limits, not lack of importance.

title: Conflicting accounts and interpretive frames
objective: Reconcile apparently conflicting accounts while preserving genuine disagreement.
teaching: Sources may conflict in fact, definition, timescale or value judgement. Before declaring contradiction, align the units of comparison. A synthesis must not erase residual disagreement to create artificial consensus. Distinguish an explanation of why two judgements differ from a demonstration that either judgement is correct.
reading: One historian describes the reform as a decisive break; another stresses the persistence of older institutions. The first examines legal authority over a decade, the second everyday administration over a generation. Their claims can coexist at those different scales. Yet a genuine disagreement remains over which scale should dominate the overall interpretation. A synthesis that announces complete agreement would be as misleading as one claiming that the historians contradict each other on every fact. The productive comparison separates compatible observations from competing judgements about historical significance.
comprehension: Which difference helps reconcile the observations?
Different objects and timescales of analysis
Legal authority over a decade and administration over a generation may show different patterns.
Which scale should determine the overall interpretation
The residual dispute concerns interpretive priority, not every factual observation.
grammar: Complete with although or because: The observations are compatible, ___ the interpretations differ.
although
Although introduces a concessive finite clause; the differing interpretations do not prevent compatible observations.
Rewrite with neither...nor: The accounts are not identical. They are not wholly contradictory. Begin: The accounts are neither...
The accounts are neither identical nor wholly contradictory.
Neither...nor preserves the two rejected extremes.
dialogue: Moderator: So both historians really mean the same thing. You want to acknowledge compatibility without inventing consensus.
interaction: Choose the faithful synthesis.
Their observations can coexist, but they still differ over which scale should guide the overall judgement.
Yes, they agree on every interpretive question.
No two accounts can ever be compared.
The response retains the distinction between compatible facts and competing significance judgements.
listening: The two forecasts are often presented as rivals. One assumes current policy continues; the other assumes the announced reforms are implemented. Their divergence is therefore partly conditional. Whether those reforms are credible is a further question, not something the comparison alone resolves.
listening_questions: Why do the forecasts partly diverge?
The scenarios differ over implementation of reforms.
Whether reforms will credibly be implemented
Whether either forecast has a condition
Aligning assumptions does not establish the credibility of the reforms.

title: Faithful reformulation and final synthesis
objective: Reformulate dense arguments for different audiences while preserving qualifications.
teaching: Expert reformulation changes expression without silently changing scope, attribution or certainty. Make the argumentative structure visible: claim, grounds, warrant, qualification and consequence. Compression can remove examples but must preserve decision-relevant exceptions. The ability to answer recognition tasks does not by itself establish spontaneous C2 production; use the material as a basis for teacher-led discussion and extended writing.
reading: A review concludes that the intervention can be effective where institutions have sufficient implementation capacity, while warning that the available studies underrepresent fragile settings. A policy brief compresses this to 'the intervention is effective everywhere except where institutions fail'. The rewrite changes a conditional finding into a near-universal claim and turns an evidence gap into blame. A faithful brief would retain both the capacity condition and the uncertainty about underrepresented settings. It could simplify the terminology, but not convert lack of evidence into evidence of institutional fault.
comprehension: What is lost in the policy brief?
The conditional scope and uncertainty of the finding
A claim of universal failure in the review
The brief universalises the finding and moralises an evidence gap.
It works everywhere; failures prove institutional fault.
It can work where capacity is sufficient; evidence in fragile settings remains limited.
It has been proven ineffective in all fragile settings.
This preserves both the enabling condition and the stated evidential limitation.
grammar: Complete: Absence of evidence should not be construed ___ evidence of fault.
as
Construe as means interpret as; the sentence warns against that substitution.
Rewrite with only if, keeping normal clause order: It can work when sufficient capacity is a necessary condition. Begin: It can work only if...
It can work only if there is sufficient capacity.
Only if marks capacity as necessary without guaranteeing success.
dialogue: A policymaker asks for a one-sentence explanation without technical jargon. You must retain the condition and the evidence gap.
interaction: Choose the accurate plain-language version.
It always works unless people do it badly.
It may work when organisations can carry it out properly, but we know less about places with fewer resources.
No conclusion of any kind is possible.
The version simplifies terms without removing the condition or manufacturing blame.
listening: For the public summary, drop the procedural detail, not the qualification. Say what the result allows us to conclude and where it leaves us uncertain. A sentence can be accessible without being absolute, and concise without pretending that a limitation has disappeared.
listening_questions: The scope and uncertainty of the conclusion
The speaker prioritises decision-relevant qualifications over procedural detail.
Accessibility and concision need not require absolute or misleading claims.
